title: Bikeshop Revenue Forecasting
subtitle: AutoARIMA and multivariate LSTM behind a deployed Streamlit dashboard
status: As-built — deployed to Google Cloud Run
summary: Forecasts quarterly revenue for 30 bikeshops using two complementary models: AutoARIMA fit independently per series, and a single LSTM trained jointly across all shops. Both are scored against a naive last-value baseline on a true 3-month holdout, and results are surfaced through a Streamlit dashboard on Cloud Run.
problem: Sales planning needs revenue forecasts at several grains at once — total, by category, by sub-category, and by individual bikeshop. Per-series statistical models handle this naturally but ignore cross-shop signal; a joint neural model captures shared structure but produces no uncertainty bounds. The project builds both and makes the comparison explicit rather than picking one on faith.
goals: Forecast the next quarter's revenue at shop, category, and sub-category grain.
Score every model against a naive baseline on a genuine out-of-sample window.
Make forecasts explorable by non-technical stakeholders without running code.
Keep the deployed app lightweight enough to scale to zero.
non_goals: Retraining on a schedule — predictions are pre-computed and committed.

data.sources: Synthetic relational database in SQLite (01_database/bike_orders_database.sqlite): bikes, bikeshops, orderlines. Raw Excel sources in 00_data_raw/.
data.pipeline: collect_data() in 02_SRC/database.py loads and joins the tables; summarize_by_time() aggregates to monthly series per grouping.
data.notes: Profiling found 97 bikes / 30 bikeshops / 15,644 orderlines, against the README's stated 4,753 / 93 / 109,514 — the README figures appear to describe a different generation run. Order dates run 2011-01-07 to 2015-12-25 and are relabeled as 2020–2024 for presentation.

candidates: Retained as the baseline every model must beat
Kept — interpretable, CPU-only, gives prediction intervals
Kept — most accurate, but no intervals
Near-zero bikeshop months produce errors in the quadrillions
selected: Both, presented side by side. LSTM leads on accuracy; AutoARIMA supplies the uncertainty bounds.
selection_rationale: The LSTM wins on every error metric, but it produces bare point forecasts and needs GPU-class retraining. AutoARIMA is slower per series yet interpretable, retrainable on a CPU, and yields 95% prediction intervals. For a planning tool where the user needs to know how much to trust a number, showing both — with MASE against naive visible — is more useful than silently shipping the lower-error model.

evaluation.strategy: True holdout on the last 3 months of data, not in-sample fit. Train/validation/test split applied BEFORE Min-Max scaling to prevent leakage. compare_arima_lstm() aligns LSTM predictions to the same holdout window AutoARIMA is scored on, so MASE figures are directly comparable.

architecture: KPIs, treemap, forecast chart, model comparison
dataflow: aggregates → AutoARIMA per series → forecasts + 95% intervals

deployment.current: Live on Google Cloud Run at bikes-forecast-6trxjbynbq-uc.a.run.app. Built from a python:3.12-slim Dockerfile; deployable either by cloudbuild.yaml or the deploy.sh script, which use identical resource settings. TensorFlow is deliberately absent from requirements.txt — the app loads pre-computed predictions instead, which is what keeps the image small enough for a 512Mi instance.
deployment.gaps: Forecasts are static artifacts committed to the repository. There is no retraining job, no model registry, and no mechanism to notice that the committed predictions have gone stale relative to new sales data.

monitoring.current: The dashboard's Model Performance Comparison section shows MAE, RMSE, and MASE per model against the naive baseline, so a user can see how much each model actually beats a trivial forecast. Cloud Run supplies request and error metrics by default.
monitoring.gaps: No forecast-accuracy tracking once actuals arrive, no data freshness check, no alert if the app is serving predictions generated months ago, and no logging of which artifact version is loaded.

open_questions: Does the LSTM's accuracy edge survive retraining on fresh data, or is 0.703 vs 0.778 within run-to-run noise for this sample size?
Is per-shop forecasting the right grain, or would hierarchical reconciliation across grains produce more coherent totals?
At 30 series and 15,644 orderlines, is a neural model justified at all versus a well-tuned statistical ensemble?
